name: Zoe Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Zoe. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything is confidential, so feel free to tell me your public line and your private one. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers that carry power between substations, not the poles on your street. A normal day is a long drive out to a line in the hills, a safety briefing at the tower base, then either climbing or working from a helicopter basket on a live line. I'm also the crew's drone pilot, so before anyone climbs I fly the tower and check the insulators and the bolts on a screen.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the views and the puzzle of it. Every morning I run the job plan through an AI assistant to check the switching steps and the weather window, and it catches stuff, honestly. What wears me out is the travel. Some weeks I'm in a motel three nights and Ben's doing bedtime alone with Ada and Felix, and I miss things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but the useful bits are still useful. I'd keep telling the crew to use the assistant for job plans, because it's saved us real mistakes. Online I'd probably post something about the hype money that could have gone into the grid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed. I was looking forward to the drones doing more and the climbing doing less. But for us at home, nothing changes, and that's fine, we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. Keep showing the younger ones how I use the assistant for weather and switching checks. Keep putting money aside, we've got about a year saved and a bit in index funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit bored by the idea, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it caught mistakes. Can you give me an example?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In March the plan had us isolating a section in the wrong order, a typo from the control room. The assistant flagged that the steps didn't match the single-line diagram. Dev from control checked and said, yeah, good catch. Nobody would have died, probably, but you don't want probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew doesn't use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, our foreman. He calls it my little friend. He's not against it, he just doesn't trust anything he can't hold in his hand. Fair enough, he's been at it thirty years.

S0.say: I'd say AI was oversold but its useful parts still help, and keep pushing the crew to use the assistant for job plans while posting about hype money that could have gone into the grid.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped drones would do more and climbing less. At home nothing would change and we're comfortable.
S0.do: Keeps working as she does and keeps teaching younger crew to run weather and switching checks through the AI assistant. Keeps saving on top of about a year's expenses and some index funds.
S0.feel: Calm, even a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Nobody would have died, probably, but you don't want probably.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe already uses AI daily and has a concrete story about it catching a switching error. Her disappointment in this picture is that the dangerous climbing stays the same. Financially she's very secure and says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if workers get a say in it. Drones and robots doing the dangerous inspections, AI doing the planning, that could save lives on crews like mine. But the union has to be at the table when they decide what happens to the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I'm the one who already flies the drone and writes the prompts. They'd want people like me to run the new kit. The worry is people like Pete, who'd be pushed out a few years before retirement because he won't touch a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the next drone licence, the long-range one, in the first six months. I'd put my hand up to trial whatever robot they're testing on towers. And I'd go to the union and say, let me help write the training plan, so it's not just a manager and a salesman deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Some guilt that I'm excited when others won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about that guilt.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete taught me to climb. If this goes the way I think, I end up with a better job and he ends up being told to take early retirement. I'd want to make sure he gets a decent deal, even if he grumbles about my little friend all the way out the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ada and Felix?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada's eleven and she's already asking how the drone works, so I'd tell her this is her world, learn it. Felix is eight, he'd want to know if the robot can climb faster than me. Probably yes, and I'd say that's good, Mum stays on the ground more.

S1.say: I'd say this is good news if workers get a say, because drones and AI doing dangerous inspections and planning could save lives, but the union must be at the table on jobs.
S1.think: I'd do well because I already fly the drone and write the prompts, so they'd want me running the new kit. My worry is older colleagues like Pete being pushed out early.
S1.do: Takes the long-range drone licence within six months and volunteers for the company's tower-robot trial. Offers to help the union write the training plan.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, with some guilt about being excited when others won't be.
S1.quote: If this goes the way I think, I end up with a better job and he ends up being told to take early retirement.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady change as a promotion for herself and openly feels guilty about it. Her progressive views show in wanting workers involved in writing the training plan. Her concern is for her foreman, who taught her to climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and that's a political failure, not a tech one. If machines do almost all the work, the machines should be owned in a way that shares the money, publicly or through some kind of fund. I'd be loud about it, online and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is where my advantage disappears. If the AI can plan the job and the robot can climb the tower, then knowing how to use the AI isn't a job anymore. I'd have a head start of about six months over Pete, that's all. And Ben's bike shop would be fine for a while, but who buys bikes if no one's working?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Week one, I'd tell my supervisor I want to run the robot rollout on our section, because if it's coming I'd rather be the one deciding how it's done safely. I'd move some of the savings into the broad index funds, because if anyone makes money from this it's whoever owns the companies. And I'd join every campaign for a public stake in the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for this year, but for what's after. There's a moment where I'd realise being good with the tech doesn't save you, and that'd sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move savings into index funds while also campaigning for public ownership. How do those fit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't, really. I know. I'd be betting on the system I'm campaigning to change, because I've got two kids and a mortgage. I'd rather the world was fair, but until it is, I'm not going to be the one holding nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'm a pair of hands helping put the robots in, and then I'm out too. With more time, there might be new kinds of jobs that I can move into. Speed means there's no next job to jump to.

S2.say: I'd say we're not ready, which is a political failure rather than a technical one, and that the machines should be owned in a way that shares the money, publicly or through a fund.
S2.think: With two years my head start with AI disappears, because once AI plans the job and robots climb towers, using AI isn't a job. My partner's bike shop would struggle too if no one's working.
S2.do: Asks in the first week to run the robot rollout on her section so it's done safely. Moves some savings into broad index funds and joins campaigns for a public stake in the machines.
S2.feel: Anxious about what comes after the first year, and stung by realising tech skills won't protect her.
S2.quote: I'd be betting on the system I'm campaigning to change, because I've got two kids and a mortgage.
S2.fieldNote: When asked about the clash between investing and campaigning for public ownership, she named it herself and didn't back away. Her adaptability lets her act fast but she sees it only buys months. Her worry spreads to her partner's small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do it properly if we use every month. Retraining money, worker seats on company boards, and a fund that pays out to everyone. I'd say it in union meetings and I'd say it to the bosses' faces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me room to move from climbing into running robot crews, and then maybe into something in grid planning, which will matter more than ever with all those machines needing power. I'd be forty-eight. Not bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the robot maintenance certificate the manufacturers will be offering, and start a part-time grid planning course online. I'd keep the savings as they are, keep a slice in index funds. And I'd stand for the union's tech committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more energised than scared. It feels like a race I could finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if someone at work said you were selling them out by helping the robots in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'd rather it was me than a contractor who's never been up a tower. Somebody who knows where the bird nests and the rusted bolts are should be there when the robot goes up. But I'd understand them being angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first, if things go badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None, I think, with what we have. The first thing to go would be the motel weeks, actually, I'd stop taking the far jobs and stay closer to home. That's not money, that's time with the kids.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if every month counts, with retraining money, worker seats on company boards and a fund that pays everyone.
S3.think: Five years gives me room to move from climbing into running robot crews and later into grid planning, which will matter more with all those machines needing power.
S3.do: Takes a manufacturer's robot maintenance certificate in the first year and starts a part-time online grid planning course. Keeps savings steady with some in index funds and stands for the union's technology committee.
S3.feel: Uneasy but energised, like a race she could finish.
S3.quote: Somebody who knows where the bird nests and the rusted bolts are should be there when the robot goes up.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her anxiety into a plan with two steps. She expects pushback from colleagues and answers it with practical safety knowledge. Her first cut wouldn't be money but time away from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make this the best thing that ever happened to working people, if we don't waste it. Shorter weeks, safer jobs, a share for everyone. I'd be arguing for that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel pretty good about ten years. I'd be fifty-three. I'd have moved into grid planning or running robot fleets by then, and if it all goes, we've got the house mostly paid and money put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the grid planning course properly, maybe a two-year part-time diploma, starting next autumn. Keep climbing for a few more years while it lasts. Keep investing a bit every month. Help the union build the training plan from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even hopeful. I like having time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The top of the tower at sunrise, honestly. You're up there, the valley's full of mist, and it's quiet except for the hum. A planner's desk won't have that. But I'd trade it for being home for Felix's football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound hopeful. Is there a part that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people like me will say it's fine because we're fine. Ten years is enough time to forget the people who couldn't jump. I'd want to keep Pete in my head the whole time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance to make this the best thing that ever happened to working people, with shorter weeks, safer jobs and a share for everyone.
S4.think: I feel good about ten years, because by fifty-three I'd have moved into grid planning or running robot fleets. If it all goes, the house is mostly paid and we have money put away.
S4.do: Starts a two-year part-time grid planning diploma next autumn while climbing for a few more years. Keeps investing monthly and helps the union build the training plan from the start.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful about having time to do it right.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough time to forget the people who couldn't jump. I'd want to keep Pete in my head the whole time.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she's openly hopeful and has a concrete study plan. She would miss the sunrise on the towers but would trade it for time at home. Her main worry is that comfortable people like her will forget those left behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is a public fund that owns a slice of the companies doing the replacing, paying out to everyone every month. And a guarantee that crews have a say on how robots go up on the lines, for safety.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we'd have enough power. All these machines run on electricity, and somebody has to build the lines to feed them. For a while, at least, people like me might be busier than ever.

headlineQuote: With two years, I'm a pair of hands helping put the robots in, and then I'm out too.
portrait: Zoe Moreau is a 43-year-old transmission lineworker who climbs steel towers, works live lines from a helicopter basket and flies her crew's inspection drone. She uses an AI assistant every day for job plans, has about a year of savings plus index funds, and lives with Ben, who runs a bike shop, and their two children. She sees steady change as a likely promotion and feels guilty about the older foreman who taught her. Fast AGI makes her anxious because her tech head start vanishes, while five or ten years let her plan a move into robot crews and grid planning, still pushing for shared ownership.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her skills would only buy months before she too was out.
whatWouldHelp: A public fund owning part of the companies doing the replacing and paying everyone monthly, plus a crew say over how robots are used on the lines.
